vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: to say that something is true, without having proved it yet
to say somebody else's idea in your own words, without changing what it means
to say the same thing again, because the other person has not accepted it
from your own experience, not from somebody who told you about it
to repeat somebody's exact words, without changing any of them
to draw attention to a fact the other person has missed
the person or place a piece of information originally came from
to say something true that does not help your own side

reading.rtitle: The Sentence That Survives a Follow-Up
paras: Two sentences can carry exactly the same information and only one of them survives a follow-up question. People say the first month is the hardest. My coach, who has sent four players abroad, told me the first month would be the hardest. The claim is identical. The difference is that the second one can be checked, argued with and disagreed with, and the first one cannot, because there is nobody there to disagree with.

That is why the role matters more than the name. Nobody in the room knows who your coach is, and it does not matter: what the phrase who has sent four players abroad does is explain why this person would know. A source without a reason to know is decoration. And the strongest quotes of all are the ones where somebody admits something that does not help them, which is why a student who says the first term was worse than she expected and that she would still go again is more believable than one who only says it was good.

There is a limit, and it is not about grammar. When you report somebody, you are carrying their words, and you do not get to improve them on the way. Changing a quote so that it fits your argument better is the one move that loses everything the moment anybody checks, and it is easy to do by accident, in good faith, at speed. So the rule that people who do this professionally follow is simple: quote it exactly or say clearly that you are putting it in your own words, and never both at once.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of the text?
choices: Quoting somebody is always better than putting their idea in your own words.
A claim only becomes evidence when it is attached to somebody with a reason to know, and carrying their words honestly is part of the deal.
Arguments should avoid other people's opinions and use only your own experience.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: My coach, who has sent four players abroad, told me that the football would be the easy part.
She admitted that the first term had been worse than she expected.
The adviser pointed out that the deposit was due before the scholarship letter.
A friend insisted that I would be fluent in three months, and he was wrong.
He asked me where I had studied, and I had the answer ready.

listenings.text: The three weakest words in any argument are people say, and I hear them every week. The reason they are weak is not that they are vague, although they are. It is that there is nobody there to disagree with. If you tell me that people say the first month is the hardest, I can simply reply that other people say the opposite, and we are both finished, because neither of us has said anything that can be checked. Now watch what happens when you attach a person. My coach, who has sent four players abroad, told me the first month would be the hardest. That is a sentence I have to answer. And notice which half is doing the work: it is not the name, because I do not know your coach. It is the role. Who has sent four players abroad is the part that explains why this person would know anything, and without it the name is decoration. One warning, and it is the one I care most about. When you carry somebody else's words, you do not get to improve them on the way. An argument you win by making somebody's quote slightly better than it was is an argument you lose completely the first time anybody checks.

Three people told me something before I left, and I remember all three because I have thought about them a lot since. My coach told me the football would be the easy part, and he was right, and he was also the only one of the three who had actually done any of this. A friend told me I would be fluent in three months. He said it twice, because I did not believe him the first time, and he had never left the country in his life. And an adviser at school told me to sort the paperwork out early, which sounded boring and was the most useful sentence of the three. Obviously the one I believed was the friend, because it was the one I wanted to hear, and that is the honest answer to why. So the thing I do now is very small. Before I take advice from anybody, I ask them how they know. Four seconds. And it separates the people who have done the thing from the people who have opinions about the thing, and it turns out those are almost never the same group.
